articles.title: What is Trailwave?
articles.summary: Trailwave helps you find, review, map, spot, tune, and log live Parks on the Air activity.
paragraphs: Trailwave is a desktop app for POTA hunters. It shows the live spot feed in card, list, and map views so you can quickly decide which activations to work.

Select a spot to open the Park Detail View. It shows the activator, park, frequency, mode, spot history, location, distance, bearing, weather, and sun or moon times when that information is available.
Optional station tools can tune a configured radio, listen for WSJT-X activity, save QSOs locally, write an ADIF backup log, and upload completed contacts to QRZ.

articles.title: What should I configure first?
articles.summary: Set your callsign and grid square first, then decide how spots, logging, and station integrations should behave.
paragraphs: Open Preferences and start on the General page. Enter your callsign and station location. The location should be a Maidenhead grid square if you want distance and direction shown for parks.

Choose your default band and mode, update interval, stale-spot limit, default spot message, and display options. These settings control what Trailwave shows when it starts and how aggressively older spots are hidden.

Configure CAT Control only if you want Trailwave to connect to your radio. Configure Logging, WSJT-X, and Map signal report options only if you want those integrations active during your operating session.

articles.title: How do I customize the spots view?
articles.summary: Use Preferences for startup behavior, then use the sidebar, search, view switcher, and refresh controls during a session.
paragraphs: Open Preferences to choose your default band, default mode, refresh interval, stale-spot limit, units, map scale, and whether Trailwave highlights unhunted parks. Those settings shape the main window when Trailwave opens.

During a session, use the sidebar to filter by band, mode, and POTA program. Use Search to match callsigns, park references, or park names, and switch between Cards, List, and Map depending on whether you want scanning density or geographic context.
Use the Sort By menu to order spots by time, activator callsign, or frequency. The selected order applies to the Cards and List views; Map remains spatially arranged.
Use Pause when you want the feed to stop changing while you review a park or work a contact. Use Refresh from the application menu, Ctrl+R, or F5 when you want a manual reload.

articles.title: What keyboard shortcuts are available?
articles.summary: Use shortcuts for common actions such as adding a spot, searching, refreshing, tuning, and marking a spot Not Heard.
paragraphs: Open Keyboard Shortcuts from the application menu to see the current shortcut list.
Trailwave includes shortcuts for Add Spot, Search, Refresh, Tune, Mark Not Heard, Toggle Sidebar, Help, Preferences, and Quit.
Mark Not Heard uses Ctrl+M and temporarily pushes the selected spot to the bottom of the visible list for about 10 minutes.
Shortcuts follow the same rules as the visible controls. For example, Tune still requires a selected spot and a connected radio.

articles.title: How do I work with the spot views?
articles.summary: Use Cards for scanning, List for compact rows, and Map for location context.
paragraphs: Cards is the main scanning view. It groups each spot into an easy-to-read card with the activator, park reference, park name, location, grid, frequency, mode, age, spot count, and badges. Each card also includes a quick Not Heard button in the upper-right corner.
List shows the same feed in a denser row format. When the Park Detail View is hidden, rows also show quick Tune, Spot, and Not Heard actions.

Map places spots with usable grid information on the map. Selecting a card, row, or marker selects the same spot everywhere and opens the Park Detail View, where the same Not Heard action is available beside the main operating buttons.

articles.title: How do filters and search work?
articles.summary: Filter by band, mode, program, age, QRT status, hunted status, or text search.
paragraphs: Use the sidebar to filter by band, mode, and POTA program. Program filtering uses the prefix in the park reference, such as K or VE.
Use Search to match visible spots by callsign, park reference, or park name. Search is combined with the active band, mode, program, and display filters.

Preferences can hide spots marked QRT, parks you have already hunted today, and spots older than the stale-spot limit. If a view is empty, Trailwave tells you whether there are no spots on that band or no spots matching your filters.

When QRT and hunted-today spots are still visible, Trailwave sorts them below normal spots. Spots you mark Not Heard are also greyed out and moved to that lower-priority group for about 10 minutes before returning to normal automatically.

articles.title: How do band limits work?
articles.summary: Set advisory frequency ranges by band and mode to filter spots and check tuning decisions.
paragraphs: Open Preferences and choose Operating Limits. Enable Filter Spots to hide spots outside the active ranges, or enable Warn Before Tuning to ask for confirmation before tuning outside them. These controls work independently.

Choose your country and license template, then select Apply Template to load its editable ranges. Each range has a band, minimum and maximum frequency in kHz, and one or more modes. Add, edit, or remove ranges as needed, then save your changes.

If your country or license is not listed, choose Custom and enter your own ranges. The limits are advisory operating guidance; verify them against the regulations and band plan that apply to your station before transmitting.

articles.title: What do the spot badges mean?
articles.summary: Badges summarize local hunting history, shift windows, and recent digital-mode activity.

content.text: Badges help you judge a spot quickly without opening the Park Detail View.

Badge availability depends on your local hunted history, display preferences, park shift windows, WSJT-X activity, and optional PSKReporter signal reports. Heard recently and Two-way copy fade automatically after a short time.

articles.title: How do spot updates behave?
articles.summary: Trailwave refreshes spots on a schedule, can pause updates, and shows clear empty or error states.
paragraphs: Trailwave refreshes the live feed at the interval set in Preferences. The status bar shows the current UTC time, the next refresh timing, and how many spots are hidden by filters.
Use Pause when you want the current feed to stop changing while you review, tune, or log a contact. Resume updates when you are ready to return to the live feed.

If a refresh fails, Trailwave shows an error dialog with a Retry option. If no spots are available or no spots match your filters, the spot views show an empty-state message instead of a blank screen.

articles.title: What does the Park Detail View show?
articles.summary: The Park Detail View expands a selected spot into operating, park, activator, weather, and location details.
paragraphs: Select a spot to open the Park Detail View. The top section identifies the activator and park, then shows weather when it can be loaded for the park.
Operating Details includes frequency, mode, spot count, and activator comments when present. It also includes quick actions for Not Heard, Tune, and Spot.
Enable Auto-open Inspector in General preferences if you want the Park Detail View to appear automatically when you select a spot. Turn it off when you prefer to keep the main view full width.

Location includes the park location, coordinates, distance, direction, local time, sun times, moon times, and a link to park details when data is available. Shift badges can indicate whether an activation is in an early or late operating window.
Last Spot shows the spotter, age, spotter comment, and a Spot History link. The activator section can show profile details and a link to the activator profile when Trailwave can retrieve them.

articles.title: What does spot history show?
articles.summary: Spot history shows previous spots for the same activator and park so you can judge recency and spotting patterns.
paragraphs: Open View Spot History from the Park Detail View to see previous spots for the selected activator at the same park reference.
History is useful when you want to see whether an activation has been moving between bands or modes, whether different spotters have copied it, and how recent the activity appears.

Each history row can include the spotter, frequency, mode, UTC time, and comments when that data is available. If Trailwave cannot load the history or POTA returns no records, the dialog shows an error or empty message instead.

articles.title: When should I use Map view?
articles.summary: Map view is useful when geography, distance, and clustering matter.
paragraphs: Switch to Map when you want to see where active parks are. Spots with usable grid information appear as markers, colored by band.
Selecting a marker opens the same spot in the Park Detail View. Selecting a spot in Cards or List also moves the map to that park when coordinates are available.
If you have a station grid set, the map starts near your QTH when no spot is selected. Otherwise it fits visible park markers when possible.

articles.title: What map overlays are available?
articles.summary: Map overlays show grayline, sun and moon positions, and optional PSKReporter signal reports.
paragraphs: Use the Overlays control in Map view to show or hide grayline, sun and moon markers, and signal reports. Clicking the main Overlays button toggles grayline visibility.

The Signal Reports overlay shows recent PSKReporter reports for your configured callsign as a heatmap. Preferences control how long reports remain visible, how wide the heatmap points appear, and whether recent history is loaded before the live stream starts.
Map scale and distance units follow the General preferences. The map also follows the app's light or dark appearance.

articles.title: How do signal reports work?
articles.summary: Signal Reports shows where PSKReporter has heard your configured callsign.
paragraphs: Enable Signal Reports from the Map view Overlays menu. Trailwave uses your callsign from General preferences, so the overlay will not start until a callsign is configured.

When enabled, Trailwave can load recent PSKReporter reception reports and then listen for live reports. The map shows them as a heatmap, with stronger or denser recent reports appearing more prominently.

The status label on the map shows how many reports are currently visible and the age window being used. If it shows zero reports, PSKReporter may not have recent reports for your callsign, the reports may be outside the age window, or the network stream may not be connected yet.

Use Map preferences to change the maximum report age, heatmap spread, and whether Trailwave preloads recent reports before starting the live stream. Signal reports are propagation clues, not confirmation that a POTA activator is on frequency.

articles.title: How do I add or spot an activation?
articles.summary: Use Add Spot to save a QSO locally and optionally post a spot to POTA.
paragraphs: Choose Add Spot to enter the activator callsign, your spotter callsign, frequency, mode, park reference, RST sent and received, and comments. If a radio is connected, Trailwave can prefill the current frequency.

Use Spot from an existing spot to prefill the activator, park reference, frequency, and mode. The activator and park reference are locked in that flow so the new spot stays tied to the selected activation.
When you submit, Trailwave saves the QSO locally first. It then posts the spot to POTA, writes the local ADIF backup log, and uploads to QRZ when those options are enabled.

articles.title: What is the default spot message?
articles.summary: The default spot message is reusable comment text that Trailwave inserts into the Add Spot form.
paragraphs: Set a Default Spot Message in General preferences if you often use the same spotter comment, such as a short note about conditions, your antenna, or the activation.
When Add Spot or Spot opens, Trailwave fills the Spotter Comments field with that saved message so you do not have to retype it each time.
You can still edit or replace the comment for any individual spot before submitting it.

articles.title: How does logging work?
articles.summary: Trailwave keeps local QSO and hunted-park history, with optional ADIF and QRZ output.
paragraphs: Every submitted QSO is saved in the local database. Trailwave uses that history to mark new parks, hunted parks, hunted-today parks, and new bands.
Enable backup logging to append QSOs to a local ADIF file. Choose a custom ADIF path in Preferences or use the default path shown there.
Enable external logging and enter a QRZ API key if you want Trailwave to upload saved QSOs to QRZ Logbook. If QRZ upload fails, the QSO remains local and Trailwave reports the failure.

articles.title: How do I import hunted parks?
articles.summary: Import a POTA.app CSV file to seed Trailwave's hunted-park history.
paragraphs: On the Logging preferences page, choose a POTA.app log CSV file from the Import POTA.app Log section, then select Import.
Imported parks are used when Trailwave decides whether a live spot is a new park or a previously hunted park.
If the import fails, Trailwave shows an alert. Check that the selected file is the CSV exported from POTA.app and try again.

articles.title: What does CAT control do?
articles.summary: CAT control lets Trailwave show radio status and tune your radio to selected spots.
paragraphs: Configure CAT Control in Preferences, then use Connect in the sidebar to connect to your radio. Trailwave supports serial and network radio connections through the Hamlib-backed radio settings shown there.

When connected, the sidebar shows the radio frequency, mode, and TX or RX status. Tune buttons become available for selected spots and send the spot frequency and a matching mode to the radio when possible.
Use Test Connection in Preferences if setup does not work. If Trailwave cannot connect from the main window, it shows a Radio Connection Failed dialog with the error message when one is available.

articles.title: How does Tune work?
articles.summary: Tune sends the selected spot frequency to the connected radio and tries to set a matching mode when possible.
paragraphs: When Trailwave is connected to a configured radio, Tune buttons are available from spot cards, list rows when the Park Detail View is hidden, the Park Detail View, and the application menu.

Selecting Tune sends the spot frequency to the radio. If the spot mode is recognized, Trailwave also attempts to set a compatible radio mode, such as CW, AM, FM, sideband, or a digital sideband mode for FT8 and FT4.

If Tune controls are missing or disabled, the radio is not configured, not connected, or the current view does not have a selected spot. Check CAT Control preferences and the sidebar connection state.

articles.title: What does WSJT-X integration do?
articles.summary: WSJT-X integration highlights decoded activators, follows your current DX focus, and can use logged ADIF messages.
paragraphs: Enable WSJT-X integration in Preferences and make sure Trailwave is listening on the same IP address and port that WSJT-X sends to.

When Trailwave receives decode text that matches an activator in the live spot feed, it marks that spot as Heard recently and can ask WSJT-X to highlight the matching callsign. If optional PSKReporter signal reports also show that activator recently heard your station, Trailwave shows the Two-way copy badge.
When WSJT-X reports that you are transmitting to a DX callsign that matches a visible activator, Trailwave can select the matching spot so the Park Detail View stays focused on the right park.

When WSJT-X reports that a POTA QSO was logged, Trailwave can use that logged contact with its local logging workflow. The WSJT-X preferences page shows whether the listener is inactive, listening, connected, or in an error state.

articles.title: What outside data does Trailwave use?
articles.summary: Trailwave uses POTA spots and park data, optional QRZ data, weather, map tiles, and optional signal report data.
paragraphs: The live spot feed, park details, spot history, and location names come from POTA services. Trailwave also caches some location data so labels can be more readable.
Activator profile details and avatars come from the callsign lookup path used by the app. QRZ upload only runs when external logging is enabled and an API key is configured.

Weather appears when it can be loaded for the selected park. Map tiles and the optional PSKReporter signal report overlay require network access. PSKReporter signal reports can also contribute to the Two-way copy spot badge when WSJT-X has recently decoded the activator.

articles.title: Why aren't spots loading?
articles.summary: Check network access, retry the refresh, and review any error dialog shown by Trailwave.
paragraphs: If every spot view stays empty, first confirm that your computer has network access and that POTA services are reachable.
Use Refresh from the application menu or shortcut to force a manual reload. If Trailwave shows an Unable to refresh spots dialog, choose Retry after checking the connection.
If spots load but disappear from the current view, check your band, mode, program, search text, Hide QRT, Hide Hunted, and Hide Stale settings.

articles.title: Why won't my radio connect or tune?
articles.summary: Verify the CAT settings, test the connection, and connect the radio before using Tune.
paragraphs: Open Preferences, choose CAT Control, and confirm the connection type, radio model, serial port or network host, port, baud rate, and serial settings.
Use Test Connection before returning to the main window. For network control, confirm that the rig control service is running and that the host and port match.
Tune buttons are disabled until a radio is configured, connected, and a spot is selected. If the connection fails, read the Radio Connection Failed message for the specific error.

articles.title: Why isn't WSJT-X showing as connected?
articles.summary: Trailwave listens for WSJT-X packets and reports connected only after packets arrive.
paragraphs: Enable WSJT-X integration in Preferences and set the listen IP and port. Trailwave accepts unicast or multicast addresses, but the value must be a valid IP address.
In WSJT-X, confirm that UDP reporting is enabled and points to the same address and port. Trailwave shows Listening while it is waiting and Connected after it receives packets.
If packets stop arriving, Trailwave returns to Listening after a short timeout. Listener error messages usually mean the IP address, port, or local network permissions need attention.

articles.title: Where can I get more help?
articles.summary: Use this help window first, then check About Trailwave for project information.
paragraphs: Use the Trailwave Help window for setup, operating, integration, and troubleshooting topics without leaving the app.
Open About Trailwave from the application menu for project metadata and links included with this build.
When reporting an issue, include what you were trying to do, the selected spot if one was involved, your relevant preferences, and any visible error text.
